title: Sensing the World: Vision, Smell, Nitric Oxide and cGMP

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In darkness, retinal sits in rhodopsin's pocket in its bent, higher-energy isomer, {{c1::11-cis retinal}}, which locks the receptor off.
cards.why: The kink at the double bond between carbons 11 and 12 holds opsin inactive until a photon flips that bond.
cards.quote: In darkness, retinal sits in its bent, higher-energy isomer, 11-cis retinal, kinked at the double bond between carbons 11 and 12.
cards.section: One bond turns, and everything after it is dark

cards.front: How does rhodopsin's activation differ from that of a typical GPCR activated by an extracellular hormone?
cards.back: Retinal is already covalently bound to a lysine in rhodopsin's pocket, so light flips it into its active shape without waiting for ligand diffusion.
cards.quote: From here rhodopsin acts like any agonist-bound GPCR, without waiting for ligand diffusion.
cards.section: One bond turns, and everything after it is dark

cards.front: When Ruth Hubbard and Allen Kropf chilled rhodopsin so bleaching stalled partway, light drove only the first step while every later step ran in the dark upon warming. What did this show?
cards.back: Only the straightening of 11-cis retinal into all-trans retinal requires light; every chemical and physiological step afterward is a dark consequence.
cards.quote: a photon flips that double bond, straightening 11-cis retinal into all-trans retinal; every later step ran in the dark
cards.section: One bond turns, and everything after it is dark

cards.front: You mix purified empty opsin with straight all-trans retinal in a dark test tube with no enzymes or added energy. What happens, and why?
cards.back: No light-sensitive rhodopsin forms. Empty opsin combines spontaneously only with bent 11-cis retinal; straight all-trans retinal does not form pigment.
cards.quote: Only bent 11-cis retinal combines with opsin to make rhodopsin (spontaneously, with no enzyme or added energy)
cards.section: One bond turns, and everything after it is dark

cards.front: Under what two conditions does blocking cGMP breakdown amplify a cellular signal?
cards.back: Rising cGMP must carry the signal, and cGMP must actively be synthesized at that moment.
cards.why: Blocking breakdown creates no cGMP on its own, and where falling cGMP carries the signal (as in rods), the rule does not apply as stated.
cards.quote: A signal is a change from baseline, up or down; when rising cGMP carries the signal, blocking breakdown amplifies it.
cards.section: One bond turns, and everything after it is dark

cards.front: In a rod photoreceptor in darkness, inward {{c1::Na⁺ and Ca²⁺}} flowing through open cGMP-gated channels form the dark current.
cards.why: That steady inward positive current keeps the rod partly depolarized and continuously releasing glutamate.
cards.quote: Inward Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ form the dark current, leaving the rod partly depolarized and releasing glutamate continuously.
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: How does cGMP keep cation channels open in a rod outer segment in darkness?
cards.back: cGMP binds directly to the cation channels in the outer-segment membrane, with no kinase in between.
cards.quote: contains cGMP, which binds directly to cation channels in its membrane and holds some of them open, with no kinase in between.
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: In the rod phototransduction cascade, active rhodopsin acts as a GDP–GTP exchange factor for the rod's G protein, {{c1::transducin}}.
cards.quote: Active rhodopsin acts as the exchange factor for the rod's G protein, transducin: its α subunit swaps GDP for GTP
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: A mutation prevents PDE6's inhibitory subunit from clamping onto its catalytic site in a rod photoreceptor. What happens to the rod in complete darkness, and why?
cards.back: By the lesson's model, the rod should hyperpolarize and release less glutamate even in darkness. Without its inhibitory subunit clamping down, PDE6 should hydrolyze cGMP continuously, closing cation channels and shrinking the inward dark current.
cards.quote: then binds an inhibitory subunit of cGMP phosphodiesterase (PDE6) to free its catalytic site.
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: How does light change the membrane potential and neurotransmitter release of a rod photoreceptor, and why?
cards.back: The rod hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate, because activated cGMP phosphodiesterase lowers cGMP, closing cation channels and shrinking the inward positive dark current.
cards.quote: PDE6 hydrolyzes cGMP to GMP; channels close, inward positive current shrinks, the inside grows more negative (the membrane hyperpolarizes), and glutamate release drops
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: How does the rod's G-protein cascade differ from the adrenaline-to-cyclase cascade, and what cost does the rod pay?
cards.back: Transducin activates a phosphodiesterase so an existing messenger disappears rather than a cyclase to make one, costing the rod constant baseline cGMP maintenance in darkness.
cards.quote: transducin switches on a phosphodiesterase so an existing messenger disappears—at the cost of maintaining that baseline all through the dark.
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: Which two steps in the rod cascade multiply the light signal, and which step is one-to-one?
cards.back: One active rhodopsin activates many transducins, and each active PDE6 hydrolyzes many cGMP molecules; activation of PDE6 by transducin is one-to-one.
cards.quote: one active rhodopsin activates many transducins, and each active PDE6 hydrolyzes many cGMP molecules (whereas transducin-to-PDE6 is one-to-one).
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: In a suction-electrode recording, a rod carries a steady inward dark current of 20 pA, and each isomerized rhodopsin dips that current by 1.0 pA. Assuming single-photon responses add linearly at low light and every open channel carries equal current, what current flows at the dip after a dim flash isomerizes 6 rhodopsins, and what percentage of the open dark channels close?
cards.back: 14 pA flows at the dip, and 30% of the open dark channels close. Setup: drop = 6 × 1.0 pA = 6.0 pA; remaining current = 20 pA − 6.0 pA = 14 pA; fraction closed = (6.0 pA / 20 pA) × 100% = 30%.
cards.quote: recorded roughly 20 picoamps in darkness, dipping by about 1 picoamp per isomerized rhodopsin.
cards.section: The rod cascade: measuring and multiplying a fall

cards.front: What two steps rapidly shut off active rhodopsin in a rod photoreceptor?
cards.back: A kinase phosphorylates active rhodopsin, and arrestin binds it to block transducin.
cards.quote: A kinase phosphorylates active rhodopsin, and arrestin binds it to block transducin (desensitization from the previous lesson).
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: In a rod outer segment, low intracellular Ca²⁺ activates {{c1::guanylyl cyclase-activating proteins (GCAPs)}}, speeding guanylyl cyclase to remake cGMP from GTP.
cards.quote: Low Ca²⁺ activates guanylyl cyclase-activating proteins (GCAPs), speeding guanylyl cyclase to remake cGMP from GTP and reopen channels.
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: Why does intracellular Ca²⁺ fall inside a rod outer segment after light closes its cation channels?
cards.back: Closing the channels stops Ca²⁺ entry while the membrane exchanger continues pumping Ca²⁺ out of the cell.
cards.quote: When light closes channels, entry stops while extrusion continues, so Ca²⁺ falls.
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: How does falling Ca²⁺ enable light adaptation in a rod photoreceptor under steady background light?
cards.back: Negative feedback from low Ca²⁺ speeds guanylyl cyclase, pulling cGMP partway back up so some channels reopen and the rod can still answer an extra flash.
cards.quote: this negative feedback pulls cGMP partway back up so some channels reopen and the rod can still answer an extra flash
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: A mutation disables the rod's RGS protein while rhodopsin phosphorylation, arrestin binding, and calcium feedback remain intact. What happens to a flash response, and why?
cards.back: Recovery becomes much slower. Even after arrestin silences rhodopsin, transducin stays GTP-bound longer without RGS-accelerated GTP hydrolysis, keeping PDE6 destroying cGMP.
cards.quote: Even after arrestin silences rhodopsin, transducin stays GTP-bound longer and keeps PDE6 destroying cGMP until GTP hydrolysis catches up.
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: Suppose an inhibitor blocks the membrane exchanger that extrudes Ca²⁺ from a rod outer segment, preventing intracellular Ca²⁺ from falling when light closes cation channels. What happens to cGMP recovery and adaptation under steady background light, and why?
cards.back: By the lesson's model, cGMP recovery should slow and this adaptation loop should fail. If Ca²⁺ cannot fall without extrusion, guanylyl cyclase is not sped up to restore cGMP and reopen channels in background light.
cards.quote: in darkness Ca²⁺ enters through open channels while an exchanger pumps it out.
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: Why do your eyes adjust slowly—over minutes—when entering a dark room after bright light?
cards.back: All-trans retinal must leave opsin and be enzymatically converted back to 11-cis retinal, mostly in the neighboring pigment epithelium, before rejoining opsin.
cards.why: Unlike the fast shutoff steps, this enzymatic retinal-regeneration loop takes minutes.
cards.quote: All-trans retinal leaves opsin and is converted back to 11-cis retinal by enzymes, mostly in the neighboring pigment epithelium
cards.section: Recovery and adaptation: two timescales of reset

cards.front: Cone photoreceptors use the same 11-cis retinal as rods, but different opsins shift peak absorption to roughly 420 nm (blue), 530 nm (green), and {{c1::560 nm}} (red).
cards.why: By comparison, rod rhodopsin has a peak absorption around 500 nm.
cards.quote: different opsins shift peak absorption to roughly 420 nm (blue), 530 nm (green), and 560 nm (red), against about 500 nm for rhodopsin.
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: Mice carry about 1,000 and humans about {{c1::400}} working odorant receptor genes, with one receptor expressed per olfactory sensory neuron.
cards.quote: mice carry about 1,000 and humans about 400 working ones, with one receptor expressed per sensory neuron.
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: How does combinatorial coding allow the olfactory system to identify odors?
cards.back: One odorant activates several receptor types and one receptor answers to several odorants, so the brain reads the combination of firing sensory neurons.
cards.quote: One odorant activates several receptor types and one receptor answers to several odorants, so the brain reads the combination of firing neurons.
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: In most mature central neurons, opening chloride channels holds the cell near rest or hyperpolarizes it. What happens instead when Ca²⁺ opens Cl⁻ channels in an olfactory sensory neuron, and why?
cards.back: Depolarization is amplified. Olfactory sensory neurons keep internal Cl⁻ high, so negatively charged Cl⁻ flows out when those channels open, making the inside more positive.
cards.quote: Olfactory sensory neurons keep internal chloride high, so negatively charged Cl⁻ flows out when those channels open; losing negative charge makes the inside more positive
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: An olfactory sensory neuron is exposed to an odorant in a bath containing normal Na⁺ but zero extracellular Ca²⁺. What happens to its electrical response, and why?
cards.back: By the lesson's model the neuron should still depolarize via cAMP-gated cation entry, but less strongly. Without Ca²⁺ entering through the cAMP-gated channel, the secondary Cl⁻ channels do not open to amplify depolarization.
cards.quote: Ca²⁺ entering through the cAMP-gated channel opens a second channel, for chloride.
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: Which tastes signal through GPCRs, and which act directly through ion channels?
cards.back: Sweet, bitter, and umami compounds use GPCRs, whereas salt and acid act directly through ion channels.
cards.quote: In taste, sweet, bitter, and umami compounds use GPCRs, while salt and acid act directly through ion channels.
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: Both a rod photoreceptor and an olfactory sensory neuron use a GPCR and a cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channel. Why does a stimulus hyperpolarize the rod yet depolarize the olfactory neuron?
cards.back: Resting on the rule that a signal can be a rise or fall from baseline, the cascades move their cyclic nucleotide in opposite directions: light turns on a phosphodiesterase so cGMP falls and rod channels close (hyperpolarizing), while an odorant turns on adenylyl cyclase so cAMP rises, cation channels open, and Cl⁻ efflux amplifies depolarization.
cards.quote: an odorant binds its receptor, a G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase, cAMP rises, and cAMP directly opens a cation channel related to the rod's
cards.section: Color and smell: more receptors, opposite sign

cards.front: In an organ bath, acetylcholine relaxes a pre-contracted rabbit aortic ring whose endothelium is intact, but fails to relax a ring whose endothelium has been rubbed off. What does this experiment show?
cards.back: Acetylcholine does not relax the vascular smooth muscle directly; it acts on the endothelial lining, which then sends a relaxing signal to the underlying muscle.
cards.quote: Acetylcholine relaxed only intact rings, showing that the lining sends a signal to the muscle beneath
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: In vascular endothelial cells, Ca²⁺ bound to calmodulin switches on nitric oxide synthase, which synthesizes nitric oxide from {{c1::arginine}}.
cards.quote: Ca²⁺ bound to calmodulin switches on nitric oxide synthase, which makes nitric oxide (NO) from arginine.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: Why does nitric oxide signal only to near-neighbor cells rather than distant targets?
cards.back: Small and uncharged, NO diffuses freely across membranes, cannot be stored in vesicles or aimed, is made on demand, and reacts away within seconds.
cards.quote: It is made on demand rather than stored in vesicles, it cannot be aimed, and it reacts away within seconds
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: In vascular smooth muscle, nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase by binding its {{c1::heme iron}}, causing it to synthesize cGMP from GTP.
cards.quote: In smooth muscle, NO binds the heme iron of soluble guanylyl cyclase, which makes cGMP from GTP.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: How does nitric oxide–driven cGMP cause vascular smooth muscle to relax and widen a blood vessel?
cards.back: Rising cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG), which opposes high intracellular Ca²⁺ and myosin phosphorylation—the two drivers of smooth-muscle contraction.
cards.quote: because smooth muscle contracts when Ca²⁺ is high and myosin is phosphorylated, PKG works against both to relax the muscle and widen the vessel.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: A standard dose of sildenafil (a PDE5 inhibitor) is applied to a vascular smooth-muscle strip with no nitric oxide and no other cGMP-raising signal acting. What happens, and why?
cards.back: Very little relaxation occurs. Sildenafil makes no cGMP itself; it only slows breakdown of cGMP already being made, so blocking PDE5 does little without active synthesis.
cards.quote: Sildenafil makes no cGMP; it only protects cGMP already being made. Without active synthesis, blocking PDE5 has little effect.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: A patient taking nitroglycerin for angina also takes sildenafil. What happens to blood pressure, and why?
cards.back: Blood pressure can fall dangerously. Nitroglycerin is converted in tissue to NO, driving cGMP synthesis, while sildenafil blocks PDE5 from hydrolyzing cGMP, so cGMP climbs and dilates vessels excessively.
cards.quote: Pair the same block with nitroglycerin, which drives synthesis, and cGMP climbs far enough to drop blood pressure dangerously.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: Compare how a change in intracellular Ca²⁺ drives cGMP synthesis in a rod photoreceptor versus in the endothelial-to-smooth-muscle nitric oxide pathway.
cards.back: By the two cascades' rules, Ca²⁺ works in opposite directions: in a rod, falling Ca²⁺ activates GCAPs to speed guanylyl cyclase and restore cGMP, whereas in an endothelial cell, Gq-driven rising Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin to activate nitric oxide synthase, producing NO that diffuses to smooth muscle and switches on soluble guanylyl cyclase.
cards.quote: On the endothelial cell, acetylcholine binds a GPCR coupled to the Gq branch, raising Ca²⁺
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: You have an unknown vasodilator and pre-contracted arterial rings, either intact or with the endothelium rubbed off (with or without added NO). Using the acetylcholine, nitroglycerin, and sildenafil rules, how can you tell which of those three drugs your unknown mimics?
cards.back: By the pathway rules: an acetylcholine mimic relaxes only intact rings (requires endothelium to make NO); a nitroglycerin mimic supplies NO directly and relaxes both intact and endothelium-rubbed rings strongly; a sildenafil mimic blocks PDE5, so it causes very little relaxation alone in endothelium-rubbed rings without NO, yet strongly amplifies relaxation when NO is supplied.
cards.quote: Nitroglycerin (used for angina chest pain since the nineteenth century) is converted in tissue to NO, supplying the gas from outside.
cards.section: A gas that relaxes arteries: nitric oxide raises cGMP

cards.front: A drug inhibits vascular PDE5 with Ki = 5 nM and retinal PDE6 with Ki = 50 nM (tenfold selectivity). Treating inhibition as simple one-site binding where fraction inhibited = [drug] / ([drug] + Ki), what percentage of each enzyme is inhibited at a low free concentration of 5 nM versus a high free concentration of 50 nM?
cards.back: At 5 nM: PDE5 is 50% inhibited (5 / 10) and PDE6 is about 9.1% inhibited (5 / 55). At 50 nM: PDE5 is about 90.9% inhibited (50 / 55) and PDE6 is 50% inhibited (50 / 100), so visual effects appear as the tenfold margin is used up.
cards.quote: Expect a mild, temporary disturbance of vision at higher doses, when the drug's concentration approaches what PDE6 needs.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A PDE5 inhibitor also inhibits rod PDE6 about ten times less well. Based on the rod cascade rules, predict how a high dose affects the speed and size of a rod's flash response, and why.
cards.back: Because falling cGMP is the rod's signal and PDE6 produces that fall, partial PDE6 inhibition slows cGMP breakdown after a flash, making the response slower. Response size need not shrink much—and retinal recordings disagree depending on dose and flash—because blocking PDE6 also slows resting dark cGMP breakdown, leaving more channels open in darkness.
cards.quote: Block PDE6 partway and transducin switches on a weaker enzyme. After a flash cGMP falls more slowly, and the response is slower.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How can the same cGMP phosphodiesterase inhibitor amplify signaling in vascular smooth muscle while disturbing signaling in rod photoreceptors?
cards.back: Resting on the rule that a signal can be a rise or a fall from baseline, rising cGMP is the relaxation signal in smooth muscle (where PDE is the off-switch, so blocking it amplifies the signal), whereas falling cGMP is the light signal in rods (where PDE generates the fall, so blocking it slows and disturbs the response).
cards.quote: The same inhibitor amplifies one signal and disturbs the other, because the two cells give opposite meanings to the same messenger.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Jeremy Nathans and colleagues isolated the three human cone pigment genes using the bovine rhodopsin gene as a probe. What sequence relationship allowed a cow rod gene to pull out human cone genes?
cards.back: Each human cone pigment is about 41 percent identical to rhodopsin, providing enough sequence similarity for the bovine rhodopsin probe to isolate the cone pigment genes.
cards.quote: isolated the three human cone pigment genes using the bovine rhodopsin gene as a probe.
cards.section: Cloning the cone pigments and red-green color blindness

cards.front: Why is red-green color blindness common in men?
cards.back: The red and green cone pigment genes are 96 percent identical and lie side by side on the X chromosome, so they easily mispair when chromosomes exchange segments.
cards.quote: The red and green pigments are 96 percent identical to each other, and their genes lie side by side on the X chromosome
cards.section: Cloning the cone pigments and red-green color blindness

cards.front: Why was the endothelial relaxing signal Furchgott and Zawadzki saw in 1980 hard to identify, and what had Ferid Murad's group found three years earlier?
cards.back: The signal lasted only seconds, which made it hard to identify. In 1977 Murad's group had found that nitroglycerin and NO gas both switch on guanylyl cyclase, which makes cGMP; in 1986 Furchgott proposed that the relaxing factor is NO.
cards.quote: The relaxing signal Furchgott and Zawadzki observed in 1980 lasted only seconds, making it hard to identify.
cards.section: How three lines of work identified nitric oxide
